name: Palmitoyl tripeptide-8

lead: Palmitoyl tripeptide-8, sold as Neutrazen, is a lab-made peptide used in products for sensitive, red or irritated skin. People use it to calm irritation and reduce visible redness so the complexion looks more even.

Suppliers describe it as dampening inflammatory signalling in skin, which means less visible redness and discomfort. It has been identified among peptides used in facial products for sensitive skin. Published research is laboratory work or tests of blended formulas, including its use as a targeting molecule for the melanocortin 1 receptor in liposome delivery; no standalone human trial was found.

paras: It is applied in leave-on creams and serums made for sensitive or redness-prone skin, usually as part of a gentle daily routine. Calming effects from such products are generally noticed over days to weeks.
Product labels advise a patch test and stopping use if irritation occurs. No specific adverse-effect literature was found.

angle.text: Palmitoyl tripeptide-8 (Neutrazen) is a soothing peptide used in products for sensitive or reddish skin, aimed at calmer, more even-looking skin. It is described as dampening skin inflammatory signals, which reduces visible redness. Published research is laboratory and multi-ingredient formula work.

lead: Palmitoyl tripeptide-8, marketed under the supplier name Neutrazen, is a synthetic lipopeptide used in cosmetics for sensitive or redness-prone skin. It is promoted as calming irritation-related redness and discomfort, so that reactive skin looks calmer and more even.[1][2]

It has been identified among the peptides used in facial products for sensitive skin.[1] A survey of 88 facial products for sensitive skin from multinational brands found peptides in 17 percent of them, with palmitoyl tripeptide-8 among seven peptides identified.[1] Published evidence on its own effects is limited to formulation and laboratory work, often in multi-ingredient products.[3][4][5]
infobox: Serums, creams and mists for sensitive skin [1][6]
Cosmetic ingredient; appears in a US-listed topical mist label [6]

paras: Surveys of cosmetic products labelled for sensitive skin catalogue synthetic peptides among their active ingredients.[1][2] In the 88-product survey peptides appeared in 17 percent of products: acetyl dipeptide-1 cetyl ester, palmitoyl tripeptide-8, acetyl tetrapeptide-15, palmitoyl tripeptide-5, acetyl hexapeptide-49, palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 and palmitoyl oligopeptide.[1] Suppliers describe palmitoyl tripeptide-8 as an anti-inflammatory, soothing peptide.[1]

A US drug-label listing for a facial mist containing it directs users to mist it onto cleansed skin from 15 to 20 cm, close the eyes, let it absorb or pat it in, and follow with the normal routine; it advises a patch test, avoiding eye contact, and stopping use if irritation occurs.[6]

The sensitive-skin peptide review notes that, of the seven peptides found, three act through a neurotransmitter-inhibiting mechanism and three are signal peptides. Only five of the seven have evidence supporting their use in sensitive skin, only one clinical study included volunteers with that condition, and the available data are mostly in patents and supplier brochures rather than randomised placebo-controlled studies.[1]

A companion survey of 88 pharmacy-channel products for sensitive, reactive or intolerant skin found niacinamide the most common active, followed by Avena sativa, allantoin, glycyrrhetinic acid and Laminaria ochroleuca, and concluded that clinical studies on these actives remain sparse and of limited methodological quality.[2]
No studies found testing palmitoyl tripeptide-8 alone in people.

Related laboratory work includes a 2025 study that conjugated the peptide to liposomes to target melanocytes carrying the melanocortin 1 receptor for delivery of the skin-whitening agent glabridin. Uptake was 1.9-fold and 3.4-fold higher in melanocytes than in fibroblasts and HaCaT cells, and the liposomes outperformed glabridin alone and glabridin mixed with the peptide in in vitro and in vivo skin-whitening tests.[3] A 2025 laboratory study used human keratinocyte and fibroblast co-cultures to test a dermofunctional base containing a Cleome gynandra extract, palmitoyl tripeptide-8, bisabolol and hyaluronic acid; the base showed no cytotoxicity up to 10 percent and lowered inflammatory mediators IL-6 and TNF-alpha and matrix-degrading enzymes MMP-1, -3 and -13.[4] These do not test the peptide alone in people.

The same Cleoderm base has been studied for compatibility with active ingredients: a 2024 compounding study found beyond-use dates of 180 days at room temperature for formulations with adapalene 0.1 percent, dapsone 5 to 10 percent or hydroquinone 10 percent, with no physical changes and preserved chemical stability.[5]

Product labels advise a patch test, avoiding contact with the eyes, stopping use if irritation occurs, and not using the product if allergic to any ingredient.[6] No specific adverse-effect literature on the peptide was found.
